title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 314: Space and Mind: Architecture & Brain
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 314 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

Space and Mind: The Cognitive Ergonomics of Architecture

Paragraph 1. For over a hundred years, builders followed one famous rule: a building only needs to work well. If an office had enough desks, good heating, and safe fire exits, people called the design a success. However, brain scientist Dr. Colin Ellard shows that buildings also change how our brains work, how we feel, and how much stress we carry.

Paragraph 2. Dr. Ellard studies how room shape changes human thinking. One interesting finding is about ceiling height. In lab tests, people sitting in rooms with high ceilings (three metres or higher) did much better on creative tasks and big-picture ideas. On the other hand, people in rooms with low ceilings focused better on small details and careful checking work.

Paragraph 3. Outside building walls also affect how pedestrians feel on city streets. In New York, Berlin, and London, Ellard gave walkers special skin sensors and eye glasses. When people walked past long, plain glass walls or blank concrete walls, their hearts slowed down and they felt deeply bored and stressed. However, old streets with interesting shop windows, varied doors, and rich textures made walkers feel curious and happy.

Paragraph 4. For decades, builders chose cheap, plain glass buildings to save money. Ellard warns that boring city streets make people feel lonely and stressed. Good buildings are never just background boxes; they quietly shape how happy and healthy our whole city feels.

groups.title: Questions 1–4
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

groups.title: Questions 5–8
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

q1.text: In the past, how did people judge if an office building was successful?
options: A. By checking if the walls had bright paintings
B. By asking walkers if they felt curious outside
C. By seeing if it had enough desks, heating, and fire safety
D. By measuring the stress levels of every worker

steps: Đoạn 1: Trước đây chỉ cần đủ bàn làm việc, lò sưởi tốt và lối thoát hiểm an toàn là thành công.

q2.text: According to Paragraph 2, high ceilings help people perform better at
options: A. creative thinking and big ideas
C. sleeping quietly during lunch breaks
D. walking faster across office rooms

steps: Đoạn 2: Trần cao giúp làm tốt hơn các nhiệm vụ sáng tạo và ý tưởng lớn.

q3.text: How did walkers react when passing long, plain glass or concrete walls?
options: A. They felt excited and curious.
B. They felt deeply bored and stressed.
C. They stopped to look at shop windows.
D. Their hearts beat much faster.

steps: Đoạn 3: Nhịp tim chậm lại, cảm thấy rất chán nản và căng thẳng.

q4.text: What problem does Ellard warn about in the final paragraph?
options: A. Glass buildings are too expensive to heat in winter.
B. Old streets have too many small shop doors.
C. Office workers dislike working near big windows.
D. Boring, cheap city buildings make residents feel lonely and stressed.

steps: Đoạn 4: Đường phố nhàm chán khiến cư dân cảm thấy cô đơn và căng thẳng.

q5.text: Rooms with ceilings of three metres or more helped participants think creatively.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...rooms with high ceilings (three metres or higher) did much better on creative tasks..."

q6.text: Low ceilings are best for big, abstract creative tasks.

steps: Đoạn 2: Trần thấp giúp tập trung vào chi tiết nhỏ (small details), không phải sáng tạo bao quát.

q7.text: Ellard's walking test in London cost more money than the test in Berlin.

steps: Đoạn 3: Có nhắc 3 thành phố New York, Berlin, London nhưng không so sánh chi phí giữa các nơi.

q8.text: Ellard believes buildings affect the mood and health of an entire city.

steps: Đoạn 4: "...quietly shape how happy and healthy our whole city feels."
